Hardware Setup of the Electrochemical Platform
Overview

The electrochemical platform is designed for the autonomous optimization of catalysts towards hydrogen isotope separation during the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) (Figure S1A). The platform consists of six modules for catalyst synthesis through electrodeposition, as well as its performance evaluation. These modules include the electrode storage module, the material transfer module, the electrodeposition module for the synthesis of catalysts, the catalyst post-treatment module, the electrochemical testing module, and the mass spectrometry testing module. Altogether, these modules form an integrated electrochemical system for catalyst preparation, post-treatment, and characterization.

Figure S1. Electrochemical automation platform. (A) The overall setup of the robotic platform for electrocatalysis. The platform includes (a) the material transport module with four-axis robotic arm (MG400), (b) a working electrode storage module, (c) a rotating module to change the orientation of the working electrodes, (d) an electrodeposition module containing four cells for parallel experimentation, (e) catalyst post-treatment module with drying unit to store synthesized catalysts, (f) electrochemical testing module using a H-type electrolytic cell, (g) a series of syringe pumps, switching valves, and peristaltic pumps for liquid handling, (h) stock solutions of metal precursor solution, sodium citrate solution, etc., (i) a catalyst post-treatment module to wash the electrodes, (j) a mass spectrometry testing module, (k) an eight-channel potentiostat, and (l) an in-line mass spectrometer for gas detection. (B) Workflow of the electrochemical automation platform.

The workflow of the platform is outlined as follows (Figure S1B): Upon receiving experimental instructions from the host computer, all instruments are initialized, and the response of H2 and HD of the mass spectrometry is calibrated. The four-axis robotic arm then takes the working electrode from the electrode storage module and places it into the 3D printed single-chamber cells for electrodeposition. A syringe pump and switching valve are used to extract and inject the solution into the electrodeposition cells. Four electrodeposition cells are fabricated for parallel experimentation and improved efficiency. Electrodeposition was performed using four channels of a potentiostat. After preparation of the catalysts, the peristaltic pumps, syringe pump, and switching valve are used to clean the electrode and the cells. Both sides of the electrode sheets were rinsed five times with deionized water using a syringe pump. The electrolytic cell was subjected to a single acid-washing procedure (acid-washing solution prepared from 400 mL water, 100 mL concentrated hydrochloric acid, and 30 mL nitric acid), followed by soaking and five subsequent rinses with deionized water. The cleaned electrode is then transferred by the robotic arm to the drying area, and the dried catalyst is moved into the H-type electrolytic cell. Finally, the electrochemical performance and H/D separation coefficients of the catalysts are evaluated using the potentiostat and the in-line gas analysis mass spectrometer. The data was processed and used to establish the machine learning model, and to generate new experiments, closing the loop for the discovery of catalysts.

The system is controlled by a computer running Windows 10 (Intel i5, 32 GB RAM). The mass spectrometry testing module utilizes syringe pumps (Nanjing Runze Fluid Control Equipment Co., Ltd., SY-09S-3mL, SY-09S-8mL) to precisely regulate the flow and pressure of gas injection at a constant rate. All pneumatic devices (Airtac Industrial Co., Ltd.) in the electrode storage, catalyst preparation, electrochemical testing, and material transfer modules are controlled through the Input/Output (I/O) ports of the four-axis robotic arm (Dobot, MG400), which operates solenoid valves to control pneumatic components for translational and rotational motions.

The catalyst preparation, electrochemical testing, and catalyst post-treatment modules utilize syringe pumps (Nanjing Runze Fluid Control Equipment Co., Ltd., SY-03B), switching valves (Nanjing Runze Fluid Control Equipment Co., Ltd., SV-07), and peristaltic pumps (Shenzhen Kamore Technology Co., Ltd., KPHM100-HAB10). The catalyst post-treatment module includes custom-designed far-infrared LED light panels for catalyst drying and storage. The LEDs are controlled via I/O relay switches (Schneider Electric). An eight-channel potentiostat (Wuhan Corrtest Instruments Co., Ltd., CS310X) is employed for catalyst preparation and electrochemical testing, while an in-line gas analysis mass spectrometer (Hiden Analytical, DECRA) measures the H/D separation factor of the catalysts. The MG400 is connected to a linear rail for electrode transfer. This linear rail module is driven by a servo motor (Panasonic Industry Co., Ltd., MBDLN25SG) and controlled by a commercial programmable logic controller (PLC) (Zmotion Ltd,  ZMC406). Each peristaltic pump is powered by a dedicated 24V DC supply, with its on/off operation controlled via a relay, which is managed through the I/O port of PLC controller (Bopai Tech Ltd, COM_GAS). The syringe pumps, switching valves and the PLC controller for controlling the peristaltic pumps are controlled via a Python interface developed based on serial communication protocols. The PLC controller for controlling the servo motor, robotic arm, and eight-channel potentiostat are controlled via a Python interface based on the TCP/IP communication protocol. The application programming interfaces (APIs) for all of the above devices are provided by their respective manufacturers. All software and modules controlling the platform were written in Python 3 and are available at GitHub:  https://github.com/Wang-Group/HD_separation.

This custom electrochemical reaction platform was constructed using a combination of 3D printing, computer numerical control (CNC) machining, and commercially available components. All 3D-printed parts were designed using SolidWorks 2023 CAD software and printed with Bambu PLA basic, Bambu PLA-CF, and Wenext R4600 resin materials. Custom metal components were fabricated through CNC machining. All CAD files, control scripts, and data-processing codes associated with the platform are available in the accompanying GitHub repository.
Mass Spectrometry Testing Module

The mass spectrometry testing module is shown in Figure S2. Since mass spectrometric analysis requires a constant injection flow and pressure, as well as appropriate system humidity, the N₂ carrier gas flow was precisely controlled at 20 mL/min using a mass flow controller, while a high-precision syringe pump was employed for sample injection, thereby ensuring reliable data acquisition. In addition, the calibration curve of the mass spectrometer was remeasured after each instrument restart. In the area of Figure S2A(a), three gas bags are manually prepared, filled with pure N2, 0.5% HD (HD purity 96%), and 12% H2 (H2 purity 99.999%), respectively. The prepared gas bags are connected to separate syringe pumps (3 mL) as shown in Figure S2, and the connections are sealed with sealing film to prevent gas leakage. During the mass spectrometer calibration, the total volume extracted by the HD and H2 pumps is controlled to 4 mL, while maintaining the total flow rate at 4/120 mL/s. The linear response curves between the mass spectrometer peak intensities of H₂ and HD and their respective volumes were obtained by varying the HD/H2 ratio. Over the test duration of more than 24 hours, the results from three parallel experiments remained linear, with an R² value greater than 0.99, fulfilling the experimental requirements. One example from this calibration is shown in Figure S2B.

The area of Figure S2A(b) is responsible for the evaluation of the electrocatalysis. The electrocatalysis cell is connected to the syringe pump (8 mL) via a drying tube. During the test, 14/3 mL of gas is extracted for each test and injected at a flow rate of 14/3/120 mL/s into the mass spectrometer to determine the concentration of H2 and HD from the cell via the calibration curves. Each sample is tested in triplicate during the electrocatalysis, and the final performance is calculated as the average of the last two measurements.

Electrode Storage Module

Carbon paper is the working electrode used in the exploration. However, they are fragile and can easily break, making it difficult to transfer the carbon papers directly during automation. In addition, during catalyst screening, replacing the catalyst requires rewiring the electric circuits, which makes automatic sample replacement challenging. To address these issues, we designed a 3D printed shell for the carbon papers using resin as the material. The design details are shown in Figure S3. The front side (a) of the electrode exposes a 1*1 cm2 area for catalyst preparation and testing. The back side (b) contacts the circuits from the potentiostat to ensure electrical continuity. Further details are provided in Section 1.4.

Before the automation experiment starts, the electrode plates with carbon paper were loaded into the electrode storage module as shown in Figure S3. The module uses a magazine feeding mechanism, which mainly relies on the linear motion of pneumatic cylinders to transport the electrode plates. A special connector for the module was designed to work with the pneumatic cylinders, ensuring that only one electrode plate is pushed out at a time. Additionally, the module is designed with a storage shelf that can hold up to 50 electrode plates, which is sufficient for daily consumption.

Electrodeposition Module

During the experimentation, the necessary information was stored in a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file. The robotic arm transfers the electrode plates to the cells for electrodeposition. Next, the syringe pump and valve switch perform the liquid transfer based on the substance names and required volumes specified in the experimental JSON file. A total volume of 20 mL was implemented during the whole project. After the liquid transfer is complete, the system connects the circuit by pushing the connectors to be in contact with the working electrode, and automatically controls the potentiostat to perform electrodeposition for 20 minutes. After electrodeposition, the syringe pump washes the catalyst multiple times with water, followed by acid cleaning and a final water washing of the electrodeposition cells. During the cleaning process, peristaltic pumps are used to transfer the liquid to waste. All the relevant codes are available at https://github.com/Wang-Group/HD_separation.

The electrodeposition module was initially designed with a single-chamber cell for electrodeposition to prepare catalysts, and later extended to parallel experimentation to four cells (Figure S4).  The main challenge is how to ensure electrical continuity between the electrolysis cell and the potentiostat when changing working electrode plates. To resolve this problem, a structure shown in Figure S4(A)(b) was designed and implemented, whose core is a printed circuit board (PCB). The central via of the PCB is connected by soldering to a gold-plated retractable spring contact probe (33.35mm). Printed wiring connects the central via to another via, which is soldered to a crocodile clip test lead. The crocodile clip then connects to the potentiostat. During electrochemical testing, the IO system controls the pneumatic cylinder to move the spring probe forward, ensuring contact with the conductive area on the back of the working electrode plate (Figure S3(A)) and completing the circuit. To ensure repeatability and accuracy in the linear motion of the probe, springs with appropriate stiffness and rod screws are installed at the two diagonals of the PCB. Additionally, in this module, the pneumatic cylinder connected to an aluminum profile of suitable length controls two cells simultaneously. To ensure the linear motion of the cylinder and aluminum profile, linear guide rails are installed on both sides of the aluminum profile, as shown in Figure S4(A)(b).

Electrochemical Testing Module

In this module, the main process is to test the activity, selectivity, and other electrochemical properties (including EIS, LSV, and CV) of the catalysts. After the catalyst testing is completed, LSV and mass spectrometry data are visualized and processed in line. The primary characterization equipment used in this module includes an in-line gas molecular mass spectrometer and an eight-channel potentiostat (the same potentiostat used in the synthesis of catalysts in Section 1.4). Throughout the automation process, the mass spectrometer is controlled via the pywinauto library (https://github.com/pywinauto/pywinauto). The code for control and data processing can be found at https://github.com/Wang-Group/HD_separation.

Building on the electrolysis cell design from Section 1.4, this module changes the electrolysis cell to an H-type cell for performance evaluation. A 1*1 cm2 anion exchange membrane (FAB-3-PK-130, Fumasep) is placed in the middle of the cell, separating the anode and cathode chambers. The anode chamber contains a Pt wire electrode, while the cathode chamber includes a Hg/HgO reference electrode (1.0 M KOH, Tianjin Aida Hengsheng Technology Development Co., Ltd.) and the working electrode. To ensure stable flow and pressure for mass spectrometry sampling, an air vent is positioned at the upper layer of the electrolyte. This vent is connected to a syringe pump, which is already connected to the sampling inlet of the mass spectrometer. The specific design is shown in Figure S5.

Catalyst Post-treatment Module

The catalyst post-treatment module mainly includes the cleaning, drying, and storage of the prepared catalysts after electrodeposition. The cleaning device, as shown in Figure S6, consists of a glass funnel supported by a custom-designed and 3D-printed stand. Two cleaning pipelines are positioned above the funnel and connected to a syringe pump, allowing simultaneous cleaning of both sides of the electrode. Additionally, a cleaning tank is integrated into the system, where the electrode can move flexibly in both vertical and horizontal directions with the robotic arm to ensure thorough cleaning.

After cleaning, the robotic arm transfers the electrode to the drying and storage area (Figure S6). This area consists of four layers, with a maximum capacity of 4×6 catalysts. Each layer is equipped with (a) a metal sink, (b) a custom-designed far-infrared LED panel (940–945 nm), and (c) designated electrode placement zones. Each electrode is positioned under four LED lights, which can irradiate the electrodes to complete the drying process before catalytic testing if necessary.

Material Transfer Module

In the entire electrochemical automation platform, a desktop four-axis robotic arm (MG400) is integrated with a linear guide to enable automated electrode transfer. The manufacturer has developed DobotStudio Pro, a PC-based control software that includes graphical programming capabilities for managing the robotic arm’s movements and I/O operations. The core control strategy involves using graphical programming to create a Modbus slave for the robot, where each movement process is assigned a specific coil register address. The Modbus master connects to the slave via the Modbus TCP/IP protocol and writes commands to designated coil registers, thereby triggering the robotic arm to execute the corresponding motion tasks. Additionally, the robotic arm is integrated with a linear rail driven by a servo motor, extending its working area to multiple modules stated above.

Preparation of Monometallic/Bimetallic Catalysts

Despite the central importance of hydrogen isotope separation, studies that concurrently evaluate both the H-D separation ratio and catalytic activity remain exceedingly limited1-8. In this work, a combinatorial high-throughput platform was established to rapidly map composition–performance landscapes. By systematically screening combinations among 30 metal elements, the primary-screening campaign generated 561 monometallic and bimetallic catalyst records with H/D separation coefficients and electrochemical measurements. Together with 148 Bayesian-optimization experiments, the curated dataset contains 709 catalyst records. This comprehensive dataset significantly broadens the accessible catalyst space for HD separation and provides a foundation for data-driven discovery and the rational design of next-generation isotope separation catalysts.

The metal salt stock solutions were prepared containing 0.15 M metal ions, 0.2 M H3BO3, and 0.1 M NaNO3. H3BO3 was used to maintain the solution pH at 5–6, while NaNO3 improved the conductivity of the solution. Additionally, an 1 M sodium citrate solution was prepared. Sodium citrate coordinates with metal ions, altering their redox potential and affecting the deposition potential.

During the initial screening, the electrodeposition electrolyte was prepared with a total volume of 20 mL, maintaining a volume ratio of primary metal to co-deposited metal to sodium citrate at 6:1:1. Electrodeposition was carried out using hydrophilic-treated carbon paper as the working electrode, Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) as the reference electrode, and a carbon rod as the counter electrode. The deposition was conducted at a constant current density of –300 mA cm–2 for 1200 s. After deposition, the samples were thoroughly rinsed with ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ·cm) and dried under an infrared lamp for 5 min.
Testing Methods and Techniques

In the preliminary screening stage, electrochemical tests were conducted using a home-made H-type electrolytic cell. The working electrode had an active area of 1 × 1 cm2, while a platinum wire electrode was used as the counter electrode. A Hg/HgO (1 M KOH) electrode served as the reference electrode. An anion exchange membrane (1.5*1.5 cm2) was used to separate the cathode and anode compartments. Prior to use, the anion exchange membrane was soaked in 1.0 M KOH solution for 24 h and rinsed with ultrapure water. The electrolyte consisted of an 1.0 M KOH solution containing 10% D2O. During the preliminary screening stage, all tests were performed without deoxygenation or stirring. The electrochemical measurements were carried out using a CS310X electrochemical workstation.
Chronopotentiometry and Mass Spectrometry Measurement

Catalysts were subjected to electrolysis at a constant current of –50 mA cm–2 for 1600 s. After 5 min of electrolysis, gas from the headspace was extracted at a rate of (14/3)/120 mL/s and injected into the mass spectrometer at the same rate. Once the mass spectrometry signal stabilized, a second injection was performed. Each catalyst was tested three times, and the separation factor was determined by averaging the last two results. The separation factor (S) is a standard measure of the efficiency of hydrogen/deuterium separation technologies. It reflects the relative enrichment of isotopes H and D in the gas phase compared to the liquid phase during electrolysis9. Based on Faraday’s law, , under the given electrolysis conditions, the consumption of H2O and D2O is negligible compared to the initial electrolyte. During the electrolysis process, the amount of D2 produced is extremely small, almost indistinguishable from the baseline of the mass spectrometry. Linear sweep voltammetry measurement

After a constant current test for 1600 s, no other pre-activation treatment was performed on the catalyst prior to the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) test. Before the LSV test, the cell resistances were determined using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Specifically, an alternating current (AC) signal of 10 kHz and 50 mV was applied at open circuit potential (OCP), and impedance was measured once per second for a total of five measurements. The average value of these five measurements was taken as the cell resistance (R). In the LSV testing process, 90% iR (current*resistance) compensation was applied. The LSV test was conducted within a potential range from 0.0068 V to -0.373 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) at a scan rate of 2 mV/s, ensuring that the electrode surface remained as close as possible to a steady-state polarization condition. Based on the obtained LSV curves, the overpotential at a given current density was calculated using Eq. 2 to Eq. 4, serving as a criterion for evaluating the catalytic activity. To calculate the Tafel slope, the current density range from –2 to –40 mA cm-2 was selected. For each integer current density within this range, a linear fit of log|j| versus overpotential was performed within a ±5 mV potential window. This procedure yielded a local Tafel slope corresponding to each current density point. The resulting Tafel slope values were then plotted as a function of current density. The final Tafel slope was defined as the converged value, where the slope stabilized without further significant variation. All data were batch-processed using a custom program, and the corresponding code is available at https://github.com/Wang-Group/HD_separation.

Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy Measurement

In the absence of cell resistance compensation, the potential at a current density of –10 mA cm-2 is selected as the bias potential. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is conducted over a frequency range of 0.1 Hz to 10 kHz with an AC amplitude of 5 mV to obtain information on cell resistance (Rs) and charge transfer resistance (Rct) during the electrocatalytic process.
Cyclic Voltammetry Measurement

The surface adsorption characteristics and electric double-layer capacitance (Cdl) of the catalyst were systematically investigated using cyclic voltammetry (CV). Before testing, the electrochemical system was stabilized by performing 20 scan cycles at 200 mV/s within the potential window of 0 - 1.1 V vs RHE. Subsequently, CV scans were conducted for 10 cycles at four distinct scan rates (200, 100, 50, and 20 mV/s). To analyze the adsorption behavior of intermediates on the catalyst surface, the voltammetric profile from the final cycle acquired at the lowest scan rate (20 mV/s) was selected for detailed interpretation. For quantitative determination of the electric double-layer capacitance (Cdl), the current densities in both anodic (janodic) and cathodic (jcathodic) directions were recorded at 0.35 V vs RHE across all scan rates. The difference in current density (Δj) was calculated using Eq. (5). A linear regression analysis was performed by plotting Δj/2 against the scan rate (ν). The double-layer capacitance was obtained from the slope of the linear fit, following Eq. (6). The resulting Cdl values, expressed in mF/cm2, provide a measure of the electrochemically active surface area of the catalyst.

Testing Result

A comprehensive primary-screening campaign was conducted across 30 metal elements, yielding 561 initial catalyst records. The full curated dataset contains 709 records after including the subsequent Bayesian-optimization experiments. Mass spectrometry and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) analyses were used to extract H-D separation factors and overpotentials at –10 mA cm-2, respectively, thereby enabling a dual evaluation of isotopic selectivity and hydrogen evolution activity (Figure S7). Notably, CoMo and CoV demonstrated H-D separation factors exceeding 10, while maintaining moderate overpotentials at –10 mA cm-2. Considering the multi-objective optimization, four promising systems (CoMo, CoV, CoNi, and FeNi) were subsequently subjected to Bayesian optimization to further refine their catalytic performance.

Interpretable Machine Learning on Bimetallic Catalysts
Overview

To identify the physicochemical factors governing H/D separation across the initially screened bimetallic catalysts, we performed an interpretable machine-learning analysis using the complete primary screening dataset after preprocessing and quality filtering. The aim of this analysis was twofold: first, to determine whether the H/D separation coefficient could be predicted from a compact set of electrochemical and element-level descriptors; second, to extract the dominant descriptor trends associated with high separation performance. In this way, the machine-learning analysis provided a data-driven mechanistic framework connecting the large-scale screening campaign to the descriptor-based interpretation used later for Bayesian optimization. The full code for machine learning is available at GitHub https://github.com/Wang-Group/HD_separation.
Dataset

The machine-learning dataset was assembled from the primary-screening results, LSV-derived electrochemical information, Rs values estimated directly from the high-frequency real impedance in EIS spectra, and element-level descriptor data.

The machine-learning dataset was assembled from the primary-screening results, LSV-derived electrochemical information, Rs values estimated directly from the high-frequency real impedance in EIS spectra, and element-level descriptor data. Standard data-cleaning and completeness filtering were applied before merging the electrochemical and descriptor information, yielding a final no-BO machine-learning dataset of 561 samples.
EIS/DRT-Based Overview of Interfacial Relaxation

To obtain an impedance-based overview of the electrochemical processes associated with H/D separation, EIS spectra from the initial screening dataset were analyzed using distribution of relaxation times (DRT) fitting. The DRT analysis was performed with pyDRTtools (https://github.com/ciuccislab/pyDRTtools), using the real and imaginary components of the impedance spectra to recover relaxation-time distributions. The solution resistance Rs was separated from the relaxation contribution, and the fitted spectra were used to extract the total DRT area as an estimate of the overall interfacial relaxation/polarization resistance.

This DRT analysis was used only to provide an electrochemical overview of the EIS response and was not included as a machine-learning descriptor set. Instead, the DRT-derived trends were used to guide interpretation of the descriptor-based machine-learning results. In particular, catalysts with higher H/D separation coefficients tended to show smaller total DRT areas, suggesting that enhanced isotope separation is associated with lower interfacial relaxation resistance. A tau-resolved DRT area in the 0.8–20 ms window was also evaluated to compare relaxation processes within the frequency range most relevant to the observed EIS response.
Feature Set

The prediction target was the H/D separation coefficient. For model development, the dataset was divided into training and test subsets using an 80/20 split. Because the target is continuous, quantile binning was used to approximate stratification during the split, resulting in 448 training samples and 113 test samples.

The first was an LSV-derived current descriptor, defined as the interpolated current at –1.00 V and denoted as I_raw. The current was converted to mA, and its original sign was retained. This sign-preserving treatment was important because negative current values correspond to normal HER-like cathodic behavior, whereas positive current values can indicate abnormal behavior such as metal dissolution. The EIS-derived quantity used in the current workflow was Rs, estimated directly from the high-frequency real impedance and used for iR correction (see source codes at GitHub: https://github.com/Wang-Group/HD_separation).

The second group comprised element-resolved descriptors describing the two metals in each bimetallic catalyst. For each sample, these descriptors were assigned separately to metal 1 and metal 2 according to the order of the two elements in the catalyst label. Missing descriptor values were imputed using the global median across the corresponding metal-1 and metal-2 columns.

Some elemental descriptors were further converted into potential-referenced features before model training. Specifically, a sample-specific offset was defined as “E_IR_corrected_final + 0.098”, where E_IR_corrected_final is the iR-corrected operating-potential proxy. The PZC- and standard-potential-related descriptors were shifted by subtracting this offset, whereas the work-function-related descriptors were shifted in the opposite direction by adding the same offset. These transformations should be interpreted as feature-engineering steps designed to align intrinsic descriptor values with the operating electrochemical potential of each sample, rather than as direct raw material constants. After preprocessing, the candidate pool contained 28 features, including the LSV-derived I_raw, EIS-derived Rs_from_EIS, and 26 element-resolved descriptor columns.
Feature Selection for H/D Separation Coefficients

Feature selection was carried out by manual backward elimination using a tree-based regressor and the mean 5-fold cross-validated R2 score on the training set as the selection criterion. Starting from the full 28-feature candidate pool, one feature was removed at each iteration, and the subset giving the most favorable cross-validated performance was retained. This procedure yielded a final 8-feature model comprising the sign-preserving LSV current descriptor (I_raw), the work function of element (metal) 2, the M–M bond energy of element 2, the H adsorption free energy of element 1, the OH adsorption energies of elements 1 and 2, the electronegativity of element 1, and the M-H bond energy of element 2.
Interpretation for H/D Separation Coefficients

Three regression models were compared for the final selected feature set: Random Forest, Extra Trees, and XGBoost. Among these candidates, the Extra Trees regressor provided the best held-out performance and was therefore used for the final interpretation. On the test set, the selected model achieved R2 = 0.6502 and RMSE = 1.0010, indicating that a relatively compact set of electrochemical and element-level descriptors could capture a substantial fraction of the variation in H/D separation across the screened catalysts.

Interpretation for Overpotential

To complement the machine-learning analysis of H/D separation, we separately analyzed the HER activity using the overpotential at –10 mA cm–2 (η10) as the prediction target. The η10 values were extracted from LSV curves by interpolation at –10 mA cm–2 and converted to the RHE scale under alkaline conditions. Samples that did not reliably reach the target current density, or that gave unrealistically low η10 values below 20 mV, were excluded from this activity-modeling analysis.

Because η10 itself is a potential-derived activity metric, no sample-specific potential offset was applied to the element-level descriptors in this model. In addition, the signed current descriptor I_raw was not used as an input feature, in order to avoid introducing a nearly direct activity proxy into the prediction of η10. Instead, the candidate feature pool consisted of Rs estimated from the high-frequency real impedance in EIS spectra and raw element-level descriptors.

Using the same train/test splitting and tree-based feature-selection workflow, the final η10 model selected descriptors including Rs_from_EIS, work functions of metals 1 and 2, PZC of metal 2, standard reduction potential of metal 2, H adsorption free energy of metal 2, OH adsorption energy of metal 1, M–H bond energy of metal 2, and the H-D zero-point-energy difference of metal 1. The Extra Trees regressor gave the best held-out performance, with R2 = 0.6723. Although Rs_from_EIS was retained in the selected feature set, the dominant and more chemically deterministic descriptors were the work functions of metals 1 and 2, together with adsorption- and redox-related element descriptors. This indicates that the HER activity trend is not primarily an artifact of uncompensated ohmic resistance, but instead reflects systematic electronic-structure differences across the bimetallic catalyst space.

The selected work-function descriptors suggest that the electron-transfer character of the two-metal system plays an important role in HER activity. The work-function projection in Figure S9D shows that lower-η10 samples preferentially occupy a high-work-function region. This region overlaps with the work-function range of efficient noble-metal HER descriptors in the present table, including Pt (5.40 eV), Pd (5.01 eV), Ru (4.80 eV), and Au (4.78 eV); however, high work function is not exclusive to noble metals and is also found for transition metals such as Ni (4.73 eV), Co (4.70 eV), and Fe (4.65 eV). Because work function is an element-level descriptor rather than an experimentally fitted electrochemical quantity, this trend provides a more deterministic descriptor-space interpretation of activity than Rs alone. Together with the selected adsorption and redox descriptors, these results suggest that the HER activity landscape reflects coupled electronic-structure and adsorption-mediated kinetic effects as the principal origin of the observed η10 trend.

Multi-objective Closed-loop Optimization of Bimetallic Catalysts
Overview

With the data from the initial screening of bimetallic catalysts with a fixed ratio among metals and additives, Bayesian optimization was further implemented to optimize the recipes for various combinations of the two metals. The search space was defined by the concentrations of the species in the solution for electrodeposition. The process was formulated as a bi-objective optimization problem: one is the H-D separation coefficient, and the other is the capability of hydrogen evolution reaction of the catalysts, which is characterized by its overpotential at –10 mA cm–2. A Gaussian process was selected as the surrogate model, and the expected hypervolume improvement was utilized to design a batch of four new experiments (three new reactions with one reference to validate the stability of the system) in line. The robotic platform detected the new experiments and performed the corresponding synthesis and characterization of the catalysts. This process iterated until the end of the optimization.

Bayesian Optimization
Objectives for Optimization
Two objectives were selected for the Bayesian optimization:

Potential at –10 mA cm-2 – chosen as a representative metric of catalytic efficiency in electrochemical hydrogen evolution. The potential scan range was –1.20 to –0.92 V vs. Hg/HgO. If the current density of –10 mA cm-2 was not reached, a potential of –1.20 V was assigned. To ensure positive values for optimization, the actual target was defined as (measured potential – 1.20 V), so that its minimal value is 0. A standard deviation of 30 mV was used to represent model uncertainty in potential.

H/D separation coefficient – selected as an indicator of isotopic selectivity. The reported value corresponds to the average measured over the test duration to ensure stability. A standard deviation of 0.2 was assigned for error modeling.
These two objectives were jointly optimized to balance catalytic activity and separation efficiency. For Pareto front analysis, the reference point was set to [0, 0].
Surrogate Models

Bayesian optimization was implemented using the BoTorch framework (https://botorch.org), with the heteroskedastic Gaussian process (GP) serving as the surrogate model for different objects. The GPs were trained on the experimental dataset, which included reaction conditions and corresponding measured objectives. Standardization of input features was applied to ensure stable convergence.

The default GP kernel employed a Matérn covariance function (ν = 2.5) with automatic relevance determination (ARD), enabling anisotropic lengthscales across features. Hyperparameters were optimized by maximizing the marginal log-likelihood, and model uncertainty was quantified through the GP posterior variance.
Acquisition Function

For multi-objective optimization, the acquisition function was based on q-Noisy Expected Hypervolume Improvement (qNEHVI) as implemented in BoTorch. This approach explicitly considers the noise and accounts for the trade-off between multiple objectives by maximizing the expected improvement in Pareto hypervolume20.

At each iteration, candidate conditions were proposed by optimizing the acquisition function with respect to the surrogate posterior, and a batch of three experiments was selected in the parallel evaluation. This strategy efficiently explored the design space while balancing exploitation (promising regions of low overpotential and high H/D separation) with exploration (regions of high model uncertainty).
Results from the Optimization

In the Bayesian optimization, we simultaneously adjusted three parameters: the concentration of metal 1, the concentration of metal 2, and the concentration of sodium citrate, by adjusting the added volumes. Two targets were optimized at the same time: the H-D separation factor and the hydrogen evolution activity. For each bimetallic system, 28 experiments (7 batches) were carried out over a total time of about 14 hours. The procedure included 8 initial experiments with evenly distributed conditions, followed by 5 batches of optimization. The optimization was stopped once the area under the Pareto front became stable, indicating that further improvement was unlikely.

Interpretable Bayesian Optimization Guided by Machine Learning

In the preceding section, the corrected 561-sample primary-screening dataset was used to identify descriptor trends associated with H/D separation. To evaluate whether the subsequent BO search was consistent with these trends, we projected the BO-sampled catalysts onto weighted descriptor maps derived from the primary-screening dataset. The weighted descriptors were calculated from the metal-salt ratios used during electrodeposition by summing the products of the relative amount of each metal precursor and its corresponding descriptor value. The descriptor maps focus on weighted electronegativity, H adsorption free energy, and OH adsorption energy, which capture key electronic and adsorption-related contributions to isotope separation.

The background descriptor landscapes were reconstructed from the primary-screening dataset (561 samples), while BO samples were overlaid using their metal-salt-ratio-weighted descriptors and colored by their measured H/D separation coefficients (Figure S15). High-separation BO samples cluster near the descriptor region enriched in high-SH/D catalysts in the primary-screening dataset. This region is characterized by intermediate H adsorption free energy, moderately strong OH adsorption energy, and moderate electronegativity. Thus, the BO results are not isolated empirical optima; rather, they fall within the same favorable descriptor neighborhood identified from the initial screening.

This agreement provides a post-BO interpretability check for the closed-loop optimization. Although the BO algorithm operates in synthesis-condition space, varying the volumes of two metal precursors and sodium citrate, the resulting high-performing samples map onto a chemically meaningful descriptor region. When considered together with the broader descriptor-space analysis, this behavior is consistent with a volcano-like separation landscape, in which high H/D separation is favored within an intermediate adsorption/electronic window rather than at the extremes of H adsorption, OH adsorption, or electronegativity. Therefore, the BO campaign can be interpreted as refining synthesis conditions within a favorable physicochemical neighborhood, improving the activity–selectivity landscape while remaining consistent with the machine-learning-derived descriptor trends.

Structural Characterization of Bimetallic Catalysts
Characterizations

Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) measurements were performed on a Rigaku Ultima IV diffractometer using Cu Ka radiation (40 kV, 30 mA). Raman spectra were recorded on an IDSPEC AVRORA spectrometer using a 532 nm laser excitation source. Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) measurements were performed on a ZEISS Sigma operated at 15 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), high-Resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) elemental mapping measurements were carried out on a JEOL JEM-F200 electron microscope operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) measurements were conducted on a ThermoFisher iCap 7000. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed in an ultrahigh vacuum system chamber equipped with the Thermo Fisher ESCALAB 250 Xi spectrometer.
CoMo Bimetallic Catalyst

The CoMo catalyst was structurally characterized before and after the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed that the catalyst exhibited a spherical flower-like morphology with a diameter of approximately 1 μm before reaction (Figure S21). High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) reveals several dispersed regions with small lattice fringes. The measured interplanar spacings of 0.215, 0.248, and 0.224 nm are likely associated with the (200) plane of CoO, the (311) plane of Co3​O4, and the (10) plane of MoO3​, respectively (Figure S20). Raman spectra also showed characteristic signals of Co3O4 and MoOx species (Figure S18). In addition, large amorphous regions were observed, which explained why only signals from the carbon paper substrate were detected in the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Figure S16). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed that Co existed mainly in the +2 and +3 oxidation states, while Mo was present as Mo6+. Oxygen species were attributed to metal-O bonds, oxygen vacancies, and hydroxyl groups (Figure S22). Elemental mapping using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) demonstrated that Co, Mo, and O were uniformly distributed in the catalyst (Figure S21). These results indicate that the CoMo catalyst consisted mainly of metal oxides before reaction.

After reaction, SEM revealed the formation of abundant hexagonal platelet structures on the surface (Figure S17), which XRD identified as Co(OH)2 (PDF#30-0443) (Figure S16). EDS and ICP-OES measurements indicated that the Mo content of the synthesized CoMo catalyst was ~3.61 mol%, but decreased significantly to ~0.5% after HER in alkaline electrolyte, likely due to the dissolution of MoOx into MoO42- (Table S2) 21. In situ Raman spectroscopy further confirmed this transformation: immersion of the CoMo catalyst in the electrolyte led to the disappearance of Mo–O stretching vibrations at 340, 807, 869, and 929 cm-1 22,23, while a weak Co–O stretching signal from Co(OH)2 appeared at 510 cm-1 24. These observations indicate a pronounced phase transformation during catalysis (Figure S19). Similarly, XRD, and in situ Raman analyses of electrodeposited Co catalysts demonstrated that Co oxides convert into Co(OH)2 under alkaline conditions 24,25. Previous studies have shown that Co(OH)2 facilitates water adsorption during electrolysis, significantly accelerating the kinetics of water adsorption and dissociation 26,27.

The CoV catalyst was structurally characterized before and after the HER. SEM showed that the catalyst exhibited a stacked sheet-like morphology prior to reaction (Figure S24). HRTEM revealed lattice fringes with spacings of 0.215 nm, 0.248 nm, and 0.236 nm, corresponding to the CoO (200), Co3O4 (311), and VO2 (440) planes, respectively (Figure S25). Oxygen species were attributed to metal-O bonds, oxygen vacancies, and hydroxyl groups (Figure S26). Elemental mapping by EDS showed a uniform distribution of Co, V, and O elements within the catalyst (Figure S24). Collectively, these results indicate that the as-prepared CoV catalyst was primarily composed of metal oxides.

The vanadium content in the as-prepared CoV catalyst was ~10.51 mol%, as determined by EDS and ICP-OES. After HER in alkaline electrolyte, vanadium was nearly undetectable (Table S3), and SEM images revealed that the catalyst transformed into a hollow ring-like morphology (Figure S27). This change is likely due to the dissolution of VOx into vanadate (VO43-) species through reaction with OH– 28. XRD analysis of the post-reaction catalyst revealed the formation of hexagonal Co(OH)2 (PDF# 30-0443) (Figure S23), confirming that significant phase transformations occurred during the catalytic process.

Electrochemical Characterization of Bimetallic Catalysts
Electrochemical Characterization of Catalysts in 1.0 M KOH with 10% D2O

Electrochemical characterization of Ni foam, Co, CoMo, and CoV catalysts was performed using LSV, EIS, and CV. The electrolyte was purged with Ar for 30 minutes to remove dissolved oxygen. Catalysts were activated by CV at 100 mV/s between 0 V and 1.2 V (vs. RHE) until stable. LSV tests were conducted with a 5 mV/s scan rate and 90% iR compensation, and the potential (vs. RHE) was plotted against current density (vs. geometric area) (Figure S34). At –10 mA cm–2 the overpotentials followed a trend: Ni foam ≈ Co (298 mV) < CoMo (132 mV) < CoV (53 mV).

The double-layer capacitance (Cdl) was determined from the slope of the current density vs. scan rate plot (Figure S35), which was then used to calculate the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) (eq. 5-6). The ECSAs were: Ni = 11.25 cm2, Co = 4 cm2, CoMo = 13 cm2, and CoV = 5.5 cm2. CoMo and CoV showed larger ECSA than Co, likely due to the dissolution of MoOx and VOx, creating a porous structure and exposing more Co(OH)2 active sites. When plotting current density (vs. ECSA) vs. potential (vs. RHE) (Figure S34B), CoV exhibited the lowest overpotential (172 mV at –10 mA cm–2). The higher catalytic activity of CoMo and CoV compared to electrodeposited Co is attributed to their larger ECSA and greater intrinsic activity.

Tafel slopes for the four catalysts were plotted against current density, and the average Tafel slope at convergence was taken as the catalyst’s Tafel slope (Figure S36). The code used for Tafel slope processing is also available at https://github.com/Wang-Group/HD_separation. As shown, the Tafel slopes are 170 mV/dec for Ni, 130 mV/dec for Co, 155 mV/dec for CoMo, and 115 mV/dec for CoV. This demonstrates that the CoV catalyst exhibits faster kinetics. The Nyquist plot at −0.12 V (vs. RHE) shows that CoV exhibits a smaller Rct value, further confirming that the catalyst possesses faster kinetics (Figure S37).

Therefore, if the RDS involves a concerted proton-electron transfer (CPET) step, H/D substitution can change the Tafel slope, whereas a purely chemical RDS is expected to show much weaker isotope dependence. Thus, the isotope-induced Tafel shift can be used to probe the HER mechanism 29.

Based on this concept, Ni foam, electrodeposited Co, CoV, and CoMo catalysts were evaluated in 1.0 M KOH/H2O and 1.0 M KOD/D2O solutions by LSV at a scan rate of 5 mV s–1 with 90% iR compensation. At HER current densities of –50, –100, –150, and –200 mA cm-2, the corresponding potentials were selected, and the KIE values were obtained by taking the ratio of HER to DER current densities at these potentials (Eq. 9). The analysis reveals that Co and CoV exhibits a more pronounced KIE effect, indicating greater proton involvement in the hydrogen evolution reaction (Figure S38).
Eq. 9

The Tafel slopes of Ni, Co, CoMo, and CoV in KOH/H2O were 181, 92, 149, and 95 mV dec–1, respectively, whereas in KOD/D2O they increased to 149, 109, 236, and 372 mV dec–1 (Figure S39). Importantly, CoV and CoMo show pronounced positive Tafel shifts, Co exhibits only a modest increase, and Ni shows a decrease in Tafel slope in D2O. These results indicate that the HER kinetics of the Co-based catalysts, especially CoV and CoMo, are much more sensitive to isotope substitution than those of Ni foam.

Because the Tafel slope is directly related to the charge-transfer coefficient, the substantial isotope-induced Tafel shifts observed for CoV and CoMo suggest that proton-involved elementary steps, such as water dissociation and/or CPET, contribute significantly to the rate-determining kinetics under alkaline conditions. By contrast, the much weaker isotope response of Ni implies that its HER kinetics are less dominated by isotope-sensitive proton-transfer steps, or that the rate-determining process is less affected by H/D substitution. Overall, the Tafel-shift analysis suggests an isotope sensitivity trend of CoV > CoMo > Co > Ni, which is in better agreement with the experimentally observed H/D separation performance.

At -50 mA cm-2, KIE(Co) (8.22) > KIE(CoV) (6.83) > KIE(CoMo) (4.06) > KIE(Ni) (2.19). Although this trend slightly differs from that of SH/D (@ –50 mA cm–2), which follows CoV > CoMo > Co > Ni, the separation factors among CoV, CoMo, and Co are very close, all approaching 10. However, from the perspective of Tafel shifts, the order is CoV > CoMo > Co > Ni, which agrees better with the experimental results. This may be because the electrocatalytic current density is related to the reaction rate, and KIE needs to be determined from the current density ratio under the same driving force. Accurate determination of η, however, is complex and challenging, and it can be affected by thermodynamic differences caused by H/D isotope substitution, which may slightly bias the conclusions 29. It can be inferred that a larger Tafel shift indicates that the water dissociation and CPET steps become slower and turn into the rate-determining steps, which is more favorable for H/D isotope separation.

This interpretation is further supported by the EIS results. Compared with KOH, the spectra in KOH/D and KOD show a more pronounced low-frequency response and clearer separation of kinetic features for Co-based catalysts, suggesting that H/D substitution mainly affects proton-involved elementary steps, consistent with the isotope-dependent Tafel shifts.

Temperature- and Current Density-Dependent H/D Separation Performance, Stability, and Deuterium Enrichment
Temperature and Current Density Dependence

Variable-current-density and variable-temperature electrolysis experiments were conducted on Co, CoMo, CoV, CoNi, FeNi, and Ni foam catalysts. All measurements were performed in a single-compartment electrolytic cell using 1.0 M KOH containing 10% D2O as the electrolyte. The working electrode had a geometric area of 1 × 1 cm2, with a carbon rod as the counter electrode and an Hg/HgO electrode as the reference electrode. For the variable-current-density experiments, each catalyst was tested in a water bath maintained at 25 °C, and the applied current density was sequentially increased from –50 to –100, –200, –500, and –1000 mA cm–2. Each current density was maintained for 20 min. For the variable-temperature experiments, the current density was fixed at –50 mA cm–2 for each catalyst, while the water-bath temperature was sequentially increased to 20, 40, 60, 80, and 90 °C. After the bath reached the target temperature, the system was allowed to equilibrate for 30 min before a 20 min electrolysis measurement was performed.

As shown in Figure S45A, the separation coefficients of most catalysts decrease with increasing temperature over 20–90 °C, indicating that elevated temperature is generally detrimental to H/D separation. CoMo and CoV exhibit relatively high separation coefficients at low temperature, reaching 9.6 and 10.1 at 20 °C, respectively, but both decline markedly as the temperature increases, with CoV showing a steeper decrease. FeNi also maintains comparatively high separation coefficients across the entire temperature range, with a less pronounced decline, indicating better stability against temperature variation. By contrast, Pt sheet, Co, and CoNi exhibit intermediate separation coefficients with overall decreasing trends, whereas Ni foam consistently shows the lowest values and only weak temperature dependence. These results suggest that lower temperatures are generally favorable for achieving higher separation coefficients.

To further quantify the temperature effect, the relationship between the separation coefficient, α, and reciprocal temperature, 1/T, was analyzed using the Arrhenius equation (Eq.10). The resulting Arrhenius fit provides the difference in activation barriers for cathodic transfer of H and D, thereby reflecting the kinetic difference between the two isotopes at the electrode interface. Based on the temperature-dependent separation coefficients, the activation-energy differences were determined to be –6.5 kJ/ mol for Pt sheet, –6.5 kJ/mol for Co, –9.6 kJ/mol for CoV, –4.6 kJ/mol for CoMo, and –6.4 kJ/mol for FeNi (Figure S46).

As shown in Figure S45B, except for Ni foam, the separation coefficients of most catalysts decrease with increasing absolute current density, indicating that higher current density weakens isotopic selectivity during electrolysis. CoMo and CoV exhibit relatively high separation coefficients at low current density but decrease rapidly at higher current density, suggesting a stronger sensitivity to current variation. FeNi maintains comparatively high separation coefficients over the entire current-density range with only moderate variation, demonstrating better operational stability. Co, Pt sheet, and CoNi show smaller changes, whereas Ni foam displays a slight increase with current density but remains substantially inferior in overall separation performance. Overall, lower temperature and lower current density are more favorable for high separation coefficients, while CoMo, CoV, and FeNi exhibit superior H/D separation under mild conditions, with FeNi showing the best tolerance to changes in operating conditions.

2.0 × 2.0 cm2 AEMWE Experiments

Water electrolysis tests were carried out in a single-cell anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE, KMem AE01, Xiamen Kah Membrane Technology Ltd.) with a working area of 2.0 × 2.0 cm2. The membrane electrode assembly was installed in a typical AEMWE cell using nickel-plated bipolar plates together with PTFE gaskets. Before measurement, the cell was conditioned by circulating 1.0 M KOH at 80 °C for 4 h to fully activate the anion exchange membrane. Electrochemical polarization and durability measurements were conducted with a battery tester (CT5001A, Wuhan LAND Electronic Co., Ltd.) at 80 °C, while the electrolyte was fed at 5.0 mL min-1. Long-term in situ durability was evaluated galvanostatically at 0.5 A cm–2.

Cathode catalyst preparation. To enable catalyst scale-up in a two-electrode electrodeposition system, the original plating-bath composition was modified. For catalysts with geometric areas of 2.0 × 2.0 cm2 and 5.0 × 5.0 cm2, the electrodeposition electrolyte contained 0.25 M Fe2(SO4)3, 0.50 M NiSO4, 0.25 M H3BO3, 0.50 M NaCl, and 1.16 M Na3Cit. Electrodeposition was performed galvanostatically at 0.1 A cm–2 for 20 min. The catalysts prepared under these conditions showed a separation coefficient identical to that obtained from the original formulation (α = 9). Hydrophilic carbon paper (TGP-H-060, Toray Industries, Inc.) was used as the cathode substrate in the 2.0 × 2.0 cm2 AEMWE tests.

Anode catalyst preparation. Ni3Fe nanoparticles were synthesized according to a reported procedure and employed as the oxygen evolution reaction catalyst 30. Nickel foam (0.2 mm thick, Xiamen Kah Membrane Technology Ltd.) served as the anode substrate. The anion exchange membrane used in this study was KMem AM01-35 (35 ± 1 μm, Xiamen Kah Membrane Technology Ltd.). Finally, the cathode and anode catalyst layers were assembled with the anion exchange membrane to form the membrane electrode assembly (MEA).

Water electrolysis tests were performed in a single-cell anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer (AEMWE, Nanjing Daquan Zhongke Hydrogen Energy Technology Co., Ltd.). The cathode catalyst was prepared as described above, with an effective geometric area of 16 cm2, while the anode catalyst (Ni3Fe) was spray-coated onto nickel felt. Prior to measurements, the cell was conditioned by circulating 1.0 M KOH at 80 °C for 4 h to fully activate the membrane, and the electrolyte was continuously fed at a flow rate of 90 mL min-1.

Based on the temperature- and current-density-dependent separation coefficients as well as the stability evaluation, the FeNi catalyst was selected for multistage deuterium enrichment in an anion exchange membrane electrolyzer (AEMWE) with an electrode area of 16 cm2. The enrichment experiments were conducted in 1.0 M KOH at room temperature under a constant current density of −500 mA cm-2.

A multistage enrichment strategy was employed. At each stage, the electrolyte for the subsequent electrolysis was freshly prepared by adjusting the deuterium concentration based on the quantitative ²H NMR analysis, rather than directly using the collected water.

In the first stage, the electrolyte volume decreased from 900 to 105 mL. The residual solution was then subjected to vacuum distillation to recover the enriched water, which was subsequently reconstituted into 1.0 M KOH solution for the next stage. In the second stage, the volume decreased from 75 to 7.5 mL, followed by the same post-treatment procedure. In the third stage, the volume decreased from 100 to 10 mL. For the fourth to sixth stages, the volume decreased from 80 to 8 mL in each stage, with identical post-treatment steps applied.

The deuterium content in the collected water after each stage was quantified by quantitative 2H NMR spectroscopy using an internal standard method. The distilled samples were mixed with a known amount of DMSO-d6 as the internal standard. Spectra were recorded under quantitative conditions with a sufficiently long relaxation delay to ensure accurate integration. The deuterium content was determined by comparing the integrated 2H signal of water with that of the internal standard. The D concentration increased progressively from an initial value of 0.0156% to 0.09%, 0.45%, 2.33%, 12.72%, 44.95%, and finally to 98.75% after six enrichment stages, demonstrating the effectiveness of the FeNi catalyst and the multistage enrichment strategy.
